planting.note: Set container-grown plants in rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; give it room to develop a solitary trunk over several years rather than crowding it among smaller understory plants.

directions: Chamaedorea tepejilote is a larger, single-trunked understory palm from Central America and southern Mexico, grown both as an ornamental foliage plant and, in its native range, for its edible immature male inflorescences, harvested and cooked as pacaya. Give it consistently moist, humus-rich soil and dappled to deep shade, since direct sun scorches the broad, dark green pinnate leaves. It grows considerably taller than the common parlor palm, eventually forming a slender ringed trunk, so it needs more overhead and lateral space than most houseplant chamaedoreas. Protect from temperatures below the mid-30s F and shelter from wind, which can shred the leaflets.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Pot in loose, humus-rich, well-drained mix and keep in bright indirect to low light; it is a slow, compact grower well suited to interior rooms with limited floor space.

directions: Chamaedorea ernesti-augustii is a distinctive dwarf understory palm from Mexico and Guatemala prized among collectors for its undivided, wedge-shaped fishtail leaflets, quite unlike the finely cut fronds of most other chamaedoreas. It stays compact and slow-growing, making it well suited to shaded terrariums, low tables, or dim interior corners where taller palms would struggle. Keep the soil evenly moist but never soggy, provide high humidity if grown indoors, and avoid cold drafts or temperatures below the mid-40s F. Its unusual leaf form and small stature make it a favorite specialty houseplant rather than a landscape subject.

planting.note: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; its montane origin gives it more cold tolerance than most chamaedoreas, so it can be tried in sheltered spots at the cooler edge of its zone range.

directions: Chamaedorea glaucifolia is a solitary-trunked palm from cloud-forest habitats in Mexico and Guatemala, notable for its bluish-green, waxy-coated pinnate leaves that set it apart from the plainer greens of most understory chamaedoreas. Grow it in consistently moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled to deep shade, replicating the filtered light of its native montane forest floor. Its higher-elevation origin gives it somewhat better cold resilience than lowland chamaedoreas, though it should still be protected from frost and hard freezes. Shelter from strong wind and direct sun, both of which fade the glaucous leaf color and scorch the foliage.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Divide an established clump or start from a nursery division set into humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; stronger light intensifies the leaf variegation but risks scorch, so filtered shade gives the best balance.

directions: Zuikonishiki is a classic Japanese variegated cultivar of the lady palm, selected for fan-shaped leaflets striped in cream to pale yellow against deep green, a pattern that holds well on mature canes grown in bright filtered shade. Like the species, it forms a slowly spreading clump of fiber-wrapped canes and grows best in humus-rich, evenly moist but well-drained soil, resenting both waterlogging and prolonged drought. It is prized by collectors for container culture and shaded courtyard plantings, where its patterned foliage stands out against plain green companions. Protect from temperatures below the mid-20s F and increase light gradually when moving plants outdoors to avoid bleaching the variegated leaflets.
sources: Pacific Northwest Palm and Exotic Plant Society
